In [[fluid dynamics]] '''Jeffery–Hamel flow''' is a flow created by a converging or diverging channel with a source or sink of fluid volume at the point of intersection of the two plane walls. It is named after [[George Barker Jeffery]] (1915)<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Jeffery | first1=G.B. | title=L. ''The two-dimensional steady motion of a viscous fluid'' | journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science | date=1915 | volume=29 | issue=172 | pages=455–465 | doi=10.1080/14786440408635327 | bibcode=1915LEDPM..29..455J }}</ref> and [[Georg Hamel]] (1917),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hamel |first1=Georg |title=Spiralförmige Bewegungen zäher Flüssigkeiten. |journal=Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung |date=1917 |volume=25 |pages=34–60 |url=https://eudml.org/doc/145468 |issn=0012-0456}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=Spiralförmige Bewegungen zäher Flüssigkeiten | journal=Mathematische Annalen | date=1921 | volume=84 | issue=1–2 | page=148 | doi=10.1007/BF01458700 }}</ref> but it has subsequently been studied by many major scientists such as [[Theodore von Kármán|von Kármán]] and [[Tullio Levi-Civita|Levi-Civita]],<ref>{{cite book | editor-first1=Th. | editor-first2=T. | editor-last1=v. Kármán | editor-last2=Levi-Civita | title=Vorträge aus dem Gebiete der Hydro- und Aerodynamik (Innsbruck 1922) | date=1924 | doi=10.1007/978-3-662-00280-3 | hdl=2027/mdp.39015068001448 }}</ref> [[Walter Tollmien]],<ref>[[Walter Tollmien]] "Handbuch der Experimentalphysik, Vol. 4." (1931): 257.</ref> [[Fritz Noether|F. Noether]],<ref>[[Fritz Noether]] "Handbuch der physikalischen und technischen Mechanik, Vol. 5." Leipzig, JA Barch (1931): 733.</ref> [[W.R. Dean]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Dean | first1=W.R. | title=LXXII. ''Note on the divergent flow of fluid'' | journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science | date=1934 | volume=18 | issue=121 | pages=759–777 | doi=10.1080/14786443409462550 | url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786443409462550 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Louis Rosenhead|Rosenhead]],<ref name=Rosenhead_1940>{{cite journal | last1=Rosenhead | first1=L. | title=The Steady Two-Dimensional Radial Flow of Viscous Fluid between Two Inclined Plane Walls | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences | date=1940 | volume=175 | issue=963 | pages=436–467 | doi=10.1098/rspa.1940.0068 | jstor=97501 | bibcode=1940RSPSA.175..436R | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/97501 }}</ref> [[Lev Landau|Landau]],<ref name=Landau_Lifshitz_1959>[[Lev Landau]], and [[Evgeny Lifshitz|E. M. Lifshitz]]. "Fluid Mechanics Pergamon." New York 61 (1959).</ref> [[George Keith Batchelor|G.K. Batchelor]]<ref>[[George Keith Batchelor|G.K. Batchelor]]. An introduction to fluid dynamics. Cambridge university press, 2000.</ref> etc. A complete set of solutions was described by [[Edward Fraenkel]] in 1962.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fraenkel | first1=Ludwig Edward | last2=Squire | first2=Herbert Brian | title=Laminar flow in symmetrical channels with slightly curved walls, I. On the Jeffery-Hamel solutions for flow between plane walls | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences | date=1962 | volume=267 | issue=1328 | pages=119–138 | doi=10.1098/rspa.1962.0087 | bibcode=1962RSPSA.267..119F | url=https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1962.0087 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Flow description ==

Consider two stationary plane walls with a constant volume flow rate <math>Q</math> is injected/sucked at the point of intersection of plane walls and let the angle subtended by two walls be <math>2\alpha</math>. Take the cylindrical coordinate <math>(r,\theta,z)</math> system with <math>r=0</math> representing point of intersection and <math>\theta=0</math> the centerline and <math>(u,v,w)</math> are the corresponding velocity components. The resulting flow is two-dimensional if the plates are infinitely long in the axial <math>z</math> direction, or the plates are longer but finite, if one were neglect edge effects and for the same reason the flow can be assumed to be entirely radial i.e., <math>u=u(r,\theta),v=0,w=0</math>.

Then the continuity equation and the incompressible [[Navier–Stokes equations]] reduce to

: <math>
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial (ru)}{\partial r} & =0, \\[6pt]
u\frac{\partial u}{\partial r} & = - \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial p}{\partial r} + \nu \left[\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left(r\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial \theta^2}- \frac{u}{r^2}\right] \\[6pt]
0 & = - \frac{1}{\rho r} \frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta} + \frac{2 \nu}{r^2} \frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta}
\end{align}
</math>

The boundary conditions are [[no-slip condition]] at both walls and the third condition is derived from the fact that the volume flux injected/sucked at the point of intersection is constant across a surface at any radius.

:<math>u(\pm \alpha) = 0, \quad Q= \int_{-\alpha}^\alpha u r \, d\theta</math>

== Formulation ==

The first equation tells that <math>ru</math> is just function of <math>\theta</math>, the function is defined as

:<math>F(\theta) = \frac{r u}{ \nu}.</math>

Different authors defines the function differently, for example, [[Lev Landau|Landau]]<ref name=Landau_Lifshitz_1959/> defines the function with a factor <math>6</math>. But following [[Gerald B. Whitham|Whitham]],<ref>[[Gerald B. Whitham|Whitham, G. B.]] "Chapter III in Laminar Boundary Layers." (1963): 122.</ref> [[Louis Rosenhead|Rosenhead]]<ref>Rosenhead, Louis, ed. Laminar boundary layers. Clarendon Press, 1963.</ref> the <math>\theta</math> momentum equation becomes

:<math>\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial p}{\partial\theta} = \frac{2 \nu^2}{r^2} \frac{dF}{d\theta}</math>

Now letting

:<math>\frac{p-p_\infty}{\rho} = \frac{\nu^2}{r^2} P(\theta),</math>

the <math>r</math> and <math>\theta</math> momentum equations reduce to

:<math>P = -\frac{1}{2} (F^2+F'')</math>
:<math>P'= 2F', \quad \Rightarrow \quad P = 2F + C</math>

and substituting this into the previous equation(to eliminate pressure) results in

:<math>F'' + F^2 + 4F + 2C =0</math>

Multiplying by <math>F'</math> and integrating once,

:<math>\frac{1}{2} F'^2+ \frac{1}{3} F^3 +2F^2 +2CF = D,</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{2} F'^2+ \frac{1}{3} (F^3 +6F^2 +6CF-3D) = 0</math>

where <math>C,D</math> are constants to be determined from the boundary conditions. The above equation can be re-written conveniently with three other constants <math> a,b,c</math> as roots of a cubic polynomial, with only two constants being arbitrary, the third constant is always obtained from other two because sum of the roots is <math>a+b+c=-6</math>.

:<math>\frac{1}{2}F'^2+\frac{1}{3}(F-a)(F-b)(F-c)=0,</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{2}F'^2-\frac{1}{3}(a-F)(F-b)(F-c)=0.</math>

The boundary conditions reduce to

:<math>F(\pm \alpha) = 0, \quad \frac{Q}{\nu}= \int_{-\alpha}^\alpha F \, d\theta</math>

where <math>Re=Q/\nu</math> is the corresponding [[Reynolds number]]. The solution can be expressed  in terms of [[elliptic functions]]. For convergent flow <math>Q<0</math>, the solution exists for all <math>Re</math>, but for the divergent flow <math>Q>0</math>, the solution exists only for a particular range of <math>Re</math>.

== Dynamical interpretation ==
Source:<ref>[[Philip Drazin|Drazin, Philip G.]], and [[Norman Riley (professor)|Norman Riley]]. The Navier–Stokes equations: a classification of flows and exact solutions. No. 334. Cambridge University Press, 2006.</ref>

The equation takes the same  form as an undamped nonlinear oscillator(with cubic potential) one can pretend that <math>\theta</math> is '''time''', <math>F</math> is '''displacement''' and <math>F'</math> is '''velocity''' of a particle with unit mass, then the equation represents the  energy equation(<math>K.E. + P.E.=0</math>, where <math>K.E. = \frac{1}{2} F'^2</math> and <math>P.E. = V(F)</math> ) with zero total energy, then it is easy to see that the potential energy is

:<math>V(F)=-\frac{1}{3}(a-F)(F-b)(F-c)</math>

where <math>V\leq 0</math> in motion. Since the particle starts at <math>F=0</math> for <math>\theta=-\alpha</math> and ends at <math>F=0</math> for <math>\theta=\alpha</math>, there are two cases to be considered.

* First case  <math>b,c</math> are complex conjugates and <math>a>0</math>. The particle starts at <math>F=0</math> with finite positive velocity and attains <math>F=a</math> where its velocity is <math>F'=0</math> and acceleration is <math>F''=-dV/dF<0</math> and returns to <math>F=0</math>  at final '''time'''. The particle motion <math>0<F<a</math> represents pure outflow motion because <math>F>0</math> and also it is symmetric about <math>\theta=0</math>.
* Second case  <math>c<b<0<a</math>, all constants are real. The motion from <math>F=0</math> to <math>F=a</math> to <math>F=0</math> represents a pure symmetric outflow as in the previous case. And the motion <math>F=0</math> to <math>F=b</math> to <math>F=0</math> with <math>F<0</math> for all time(<math>-\alpha\leq\theta\leq\alpha</math>) represents a pure symmetric inflow. But also, the particle may oscillate between <math>b\leq F\leq a</math>, representing both inflow and outflow regions and the flow is no longer need to symmetric about <math>\theta=0</math>.
The rich structure of this dynamical interpretation can be found in [[Louis Rosenhead|Rosenhead]](1940).<ref name=Rosenhead_1940/>

== Pure outflow ==

For pure outflow, since <math>F=a</math> at <math>\theta=0</math>, integration of governing equation gives

:<math>\theta = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_F^a \frac{dF}{\sqrt{(a-F)(F-b)(F-c))}}</math>

and the boundary conditions becomes

:<math>\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_0^a \frac{dF}{\sqrt{(a-F)(F-b)(F-c))}}, \quad Re = 2\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_0^\alpha \frac{FdF}{\sqrt{(a-F)(F-b)(F-c))}}.</math>

The equations can be simplified by standard transformations given for example in [[Harold Jeffreys|Jeffreys]].<ref>Jeffreys, Harold, Bertha Swirles "Methods of mathematical physics." New York: Cambridge University Press (1956): 32–34.</ref>

* First case  <math>b,c</math> are complex conjugates and <math>a>0</math> leads to

:: <math>F(\theta)=a-\frac{3M^2}{2}\frac{1-\operatorname{cn}(M\theta,\kappa)}{1+\operatorname{cn}(M\theta,\kappa)}</math>
:: <math>M^2 = \frac{2}{3} \sqrt{(a-b)(a-c)}, \quad \kappa^2=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{a+2}{2M^2}</math>

where <math>\operatorname{sn}, \operatorname{cn}</math> are [[Jacobi elliptic functions]].

* Second case  <math>c<b<0<a</math> leads to

:: <math>F(\theta)=a-6k^2 m^2\operatorname{sn}^2(m\theta,k)</math>
:: <math>m^2 = \frac{1}{6} (a-c), \quad k^2=\frac{a-b}{a-c}.</math>

=== Limiting form ===

The limiting condition is obtained by noting that pure outflow is impossible when <math>F'(\pm\alpha)=0</math>, which implies <math>b=0</math> from the governing equation. Thus beyond this critical conditions, no solution exists. The critical angle <math>\alpha_c</math> is given by

: <math>
\begin{align}
\alpha_c &= \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_0^a \frac{dF}{\sqrt{F(a-F)(F+a+6))}},\\
         &= \sqrt{\frac{3}{2a}} \int_0^1 \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t(1-t)\{1+(1+6/a)t\}}},\\
         &= \frac{K(k^2)}{m^2}
\end{align}
</math>

where

:<math>m^2 = \frac{3+a}{3}, \quad k^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a}{3+a}\right)</math>

where <math>K(k^2)</math> is the [[complete elliptic integral of the first kind]]. For large values of <math>a</math>, the critical angle becomes <math>\alpha_c =\sqrt{\frac{3}{a}}K\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{3.211}{\sqrt{a}}</math>.

The corresponding critical [[Reynolds number]] or volume flux is given by

: <math>
\begin{align}
Re_c = \frac{Q_c}{\nu} &= 2 \int_0^{\alpha_c} (a-6k^2 m^2\operatorname{sn}^2 m\theta) \, d\theta,\\
                       &= \frac{12k^2}{\sqrt{1-2k^2}} \int_0^K \operatorname{cn}^2 t dt,\\
                       &=  \frac{12}{\sqrt{1-2k^2}}[ E(k^2) -(1-k^2)K(k^2)]              
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>E(k^2)</math> is the [[complete elliptic integral of the second kind]]. For large values of <math>a, \left(\ k^2\sim \frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2a}\right)</math>, the critical Reynolds number or volume flux becomes <math>Re_c=\frac{Q_c}{\nu} = 12 \sqrt{\frac{a}{3}} \left[E\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2}K\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \right]=2.934 \sqrt{a}</math>.

== Pure inflow ==

For pure inflow, the implicit solution is given by

: <math>\theta = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_b^F \frac{dF}{\sqrt{(a-F)(F-b)(F-c))}}</math>

and the boundary conditions becomes

: <math>\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_b^0 \frac{dF}{\sqrt{(a-F)(F-b)(F-c))}}, \quad Re = 2\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \int_\alpha^0 \frac{FdF}{\sqrt{(a-F)(F-b)(F-c))}}.</math>

Pure inflow is possible only when all constants are real <math>c<b<0<a</math> and the solution is given by

:<math>F(\theta)=a-6k^2 m^2\operatorname{sn}^2(K-m\theta,k)=b+6k^2 m^2 \operatorname{cn}^2(K-m\theta,k)</math>
:<math>m^2 = \frac{1}{6} (a-c), \quad k^2=\frac{a-b}{a-c}</math>

where <math>K(k^2)</math> is the [[complete elliptic integral of the first kind]].

=== Limiting form ===

As Reynolds number increases (<math>-b</math> becomes larger), the flow tends to become uniform(thus approaching [[potential theory|potential flow]] solution), except for boundary layers near the walls. Since <math>m</math> is large and <math>\alpha</math> is given, it is clear from the solution that <math>K</math> must be large, therefore <math>k\sim 1</math>. But when <math>k\approx 1</math>, <math>\operatorname{sn} t\approx \tanh t, \ c\approx b, \ a\approx -2b </math>, the solution becomes

:<math>F(\theta) = b\left\{3\tanh^2 \left[\sqrt{-\frac{b}{2}}(\alpha-\theta)+\tanh^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right]-2\right\}. </math>

It is clear that <math>F\approx b</math> everywhere except in the boundary layer of thickness <math>O\left(\sqrt{-\frac{b}{2}}\right)</math>. The volume flux is <math>Q/\nu\approx 2\alpha b</math> so that <math>|Re|=O(|b|)</math> and the boundary layers have classical thickness <math>O\left(|Re|^{1/2}\right)</math>.

== Jeffery-Hamel Flow with Stretching Shrinking Surface ==
Jeffery-Hamel Flow in the channel, with various effects has been studied by researchers as Turkyilmazoglu,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turkyilmazoglu |first=Mustafa |date=September 2014 |title=Extending the traditional Jeffery-Hamel flow to stretchable convergent/divergent channels |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S004579301400214X |journal=Computers & Fluids |language=en |volume=100 |pages=196–203 |doi=10.1016/j.compfluid.2014.05.016|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Ganji,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ganji |first1=Z.Z. |last2=Ganji |first2=D.D. |last3=Esmaeilpour |first3=M. |date=December 2009 |title=Study on nonlinear Jeffery–Hamel flow by He's semi-analytical methods and comparison with numerical results |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0898122109001345 |journal=Computers & Mathematics with Applications |language=en |volume=58 |issue=11–12 |pages=2107–2116 |doi=10.1016/j.camwa.2009.03.044|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Saumy Mittal,<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Sinha |first1=Sharad |last2=Mittal |first2=Saumy |date=2026-05-07 |title=Heat transfer and flow dynamics of Williamson fluid in a converging/diverging channel under surface stretching and shrinking effects |journal=Journal of Engineering and Applied Science |language=en |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=177 |doi=10.1186/s44147-026-01017-3 |doi-access=free |issn=2536-9512}}</ref> M. Mohan etc. It was observed that fluid velocity decreases in converging channels but increases significantly in diverging channels for higher Williamson and [[viscosity]] parameters. The temperature of the fluid increases slightly with these parameters, while the skin-friction coefficient decreases for both converging and diverging channels. It was also found that heat transfer is enhanced more effectively in diverging channels, especially under shrinking-wall conditions and higher Eckert numbers.<ref name=":0" />
